payload.claim: `_depends_on_refusal` computes `states` from `_rows_for`, which spans every task a dependency spec has ever had across every `spec_sha` (confirmed by `ledger.tasks_by_spec`'s own docstring: 'one key routinely holds many', and by `DONE_STATES`'s comment that an edited spec gets a new `spec_sha` unaffected by a stale task's disposition). The dead-state check then uses `any(state in DEPENDENCY_DEAD_STATES for state in states)`, so a parent that was `REJECTED` under an old `spec_sha` and has since been edited and resubmitted (a fresh task now `IMPLEMENTING`, `PLANNING`, etc. under a new `spec_sha`) still trips this branch and produces the message 'depends_on X is REJECTED, which will not reach READY_FOR_REVIEW — not merely not started yet.' That claim is false while the new attempt is in flight: the parent may well reach `READY_FOR_REVIEW` this same batch. Existential aggregation is correct for satisfaction (once satisfied, always satisfied per `_rows_for`'s own docstring) but is wrong for dead-state detection, which is a claim about the parent's current trajectory, not a claim that survives being superseded by a later attempt. No test exercises a dependency with more than one task row, so this asymmetry between the two uses of `any()` on the same `states` list is untested.
